extracted.intended_audience: mathematics education researchers, calculus instructors, and graduate teaching assistants
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and implementing a diagnostic assessment to evaluate students' comprehension of the logical structure and implications of the formal definition of limit (epsilon-delta). Includes written delta/epsilon diagram items and a probing interview protocol; intended for use after a classroom intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: We control delta, not epsilon
rubrics_metrics.description: The student understands that in the epsilon-delta definition the analyst (or function's producer) chooses a delta in response to a given epsilon; epsilon is not under the student's (or function's) control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detectable when students attempt to correct diagrams by changing epsilon instead of recognizing only delta can be adjusted (e.g., redrawing the epsilon interval to match delta reveals lack of this concept).

rubrics_metrics.name: Delta interval must fit inside (cannot be outside) epsilon interval
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should recognize that the chosen delta-interval around a must lie within the epsilon-interval around L for the diagram to satisfy the definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many students grasp this concept; explanations often attributed to contextual metaphors (bolt problem). In the assessment, incorrect pairings where the delta-interval extends outside the epsilon-interval should be rejected by students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delta interval can be strictly inside epsilon interval
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should accept that the delta-interval may be strictly smaller than the epsilon-interval (i.e., it need not match the epsilon bound).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a student corrects a diagram by expanding delta to match epsilon (as in Figure 2), this indicates failure to grasp that delta can be strictly inside epsilon (concept #3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Delta and epsilon do not have to be equal
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should understand that delta and epsilon represent different quantities and are not required to be numerically equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probe responses asking 'Do delta and epsilon have to be equal?' A correct understanding explains they describe different qualities; changing one to match the other indicates misconception (also linked to concept #4).

rubrics_metrics.name: In continuous case, f(a) = L must hold
rubrics_metrics.description: For the limit as x approaches a to equal L in the continuous case, students should recognize that f(a) = L.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students failing to note misalignment of a and L in diagrams (even if delta inside epsilon) show lack of this concept. Assessment items should include diagrams where a and L are misaligned to test recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetric interval lengths around a and L
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should recognize that the intervals (delta around a and epsilon around L) have the same length on each side because 'you can be the same distance (delta/epsilon) away in both directions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment and interview can probe whether students assume interval lengths may differ on left/right without justification; diagrams should include asymmetric cases to test this.

rubrics_metrics.name: For non-linear graphs, one side of delta interval may match epsilon while the other is strictly inside
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should understand that for non-linear functions, matching on both sides need not occur; one side of the delta-interval may coincide with the epsilon-interval while the other side is strictly inside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include asymmetric delta/epsilon diagram items for non-linear graphs to reveal whether students can reason side-by-side about differing constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delta/epsilon diagram assessment format
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a written assessment of standard delta/epsilon diagrams (author used six diagrams) where for each diagram the student must either confirm the pairing or explain why it is not appropriate and correct it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The task reveals which of the seven target concepts students hold. Example: Figure 1 (correct pairing) and Figure 2 (student correction expanding delta) are used to discriminate understanding. Non-interviewed written responses are coded as a single pass; interviewed students provide richer data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview protocol and probing procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: After students complete explanations for all diagrams, the interviewer probes responses: for correct answers test robustness (e.g., show alternative diagram and ask whether delta must be bigger), and for incorrect/partial answers probe the missing concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protocol: interview only after initial explanations to obtain baseline. Example probe questions: 'Another student might say that the delta is too small, and should be bigger to match the epsilon. Do you need to do this?' and 'Is it ok for the delta interval to be inside of the epsilon interval? Do delta and epsilon have to be equal?' The second-pass probing often leads students to articulate multiple concepts they initially missed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructional sequence recommendation (bolt problem → diagnostic → discussion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Present an engaging context (the bolt manufacturing problem) to introduce the logical mapping to the formal definition, then assign the delta/epsilon diagnostic and follow with a probing discussion; the bolt problem primes but is not sufficient alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume the contextual activity instills all embedded concepts; the researcher intentionally did not highlight the seven concepts during instruction. The recommended sequence: introduce bolt problem, map representations (problem, diagram, formal definition), give diagnostic (written homework), then conduct probing discussion/interview. Evidence: many students gained missing concepts only after the probing discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring and coding procedure for assessment data
rubrics_metrics.description: Transcribe interviews and compare verbal responses to written solutions in two passes (initial explanations and post-probe), and code written responses of non-interviewed students as if they had completed the first pass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use coding to identify which of the seven concepts appear in student reasoning and whether responses are robust under probing. Report proportions (e.g., number of students who ultimately expressed every concept after probing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment dimensions for equivalence relations (transition-to-proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing student understanding of equivalence relations, evaluate concept image, concept definition, and concept usage in writing proofs (including connections to partitions and prototypical examples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Task-based interviews aimed at these dimensions showed that small-group learning activities produced stronger connections to partitions and better success in writing proofs; concrete activities yielded prototypical examples that aided encapsulation of essential features.
